title: Air France Flight 447
one_line: Unreliable speed readings preceded loss of control, a sustained loss of wing lift, and ocean impact.
status_why: Recovered recorders establish the loss of control and stall sequence, while corporate legal responsibility remains contested.

aircraft.livery_notes: The 2 May 2009 photograph of this airframe shows a white fuselage, dark blue AIR FRANCE titles, and diagonal blue, white and red tail stripes. This is the nearest dated photograph inspected; accident-day paint details were not independently established (s14).

from.name: Rio de Janeiro Galeão – Tom Jobim International Airport

site.description: BEA synopsis reference 3°03′57″ N, 30°33′42″ W, converted by degrees + minutes/60 + seconds/3600. This locates the accident/wreckage area, not a proven exact sea-surface impact coordinate. Wreckage lay on a clay-sediment abyssal plain about 15 km wide, east of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, about 6.5 NM on radial 019 from the last transmitted position. Surrounding seabed relief ranged roughly from 700 to 4,300 m depth (s1, synopsis and section 1.12.1, pp.64–66).

environment.notes: Météo-France ARPEGE analysis, appendix 1 sections 1.1–1.4 pp.76–78: regional winds below FL180 were easterly to southeasterly and less than 20 kt; above FL180 northerly and less than 20 kt between 10° S and 10° N. These are regional model-analysis bounds, not an exact wind vector at the aircraft. Tropopause about FL520 and -80 °C. No local surface sea-state observation is established.
Appendix 2 p.1 initial-state table. Static air temperature, pressure altitude 34,992 ft. No coordinate pair is printed in this table.

environment.place: Convective cluster on the planned oceanic route
environment.precip: High-altitude cloud contained ice; particle size, concentration and liquid-water fraction along AF447’s precise path were not measured.
environment.turbulence: The satellite analysis supports possible marked turbulence within the cluster; it does not measure what AF447 encountered.

cloud_layers.coverage: Heterogeneous cluster; no measured oktas along the flight path.

environment.notes: Météo-France appendix 1 section 2.3 pp.83–91: cloud-top infrared temperatures about -75 to -80 °C; some tops near the tropopause, around FL500–FL520. The roughly 400 km-wide cluster formed by merger of four clusters. Satellite images cannot resolve conditions at cruise level. Forecast TEMSI tops FL450 (s1 p.46) describe a forecast, not the same measurement; cloud base and true-MSL top are unknown.

environment.turbulence: FDR normal-acceleration variation reached a maximum of about 0.5 g peak-to-peak in the 02:07–02:10 interval.
environment.notes: Static temperature: s2 p.1. Turbulence interval: s1 section 1.11.2, figure 24 p.58. No numeric wind direction or wind speed is transcribed from the recorder here. The BEA simulation used a 15 kt headwind component consistent with recorded wind, but that component is not a full wind-vector observation (s1 p.91).

environment.place: Last recorded aircraft sample near the sea
environment.notes: Appendix 2 p.9 last-values table: static temperature 24.3 °C and radio altitude 71 ft. This is a last recorded value, not an independent sea-surface weather observation. Visibility, waves, moon visibility, precipitation at sea level and surface wind remain unknown.

TRMM lightning imager indicated no lightning in the accident zone at 02:30 (s1 section 1.7.3 p.47). This later satellite pass does not establish the presence or absence of lightning at 02:10. lightning therefore remains null.

events.title: Departure from Rio
events.detail: AF447 took off for Paris with 228 people aboard. The captain was monitoring and the right-seat copilot was flying.
events.caption: The flight left Rio for Paris with 228 people aboard. The right-seat copilot was flying.

events.title: Oceanic position report
events.detail: The crew reported passing INTOL at 01:33 and estimated SALPU at 01:48. The final report gives ORARO estimated at 02:04, while the first interim report gives 02:00; both are retained in conflicts.
events.locator: Final report section 1.9.1 p.49; first interim section 1.1
events.caption: The crew reported passing INTOL and gave estimated arrival times for the next points along the route.

events.title: Controller requests TASIL estimate
events.detail: The controller instructed the crew to maintain FL350 and asked for a TASIL estimate. Repeated later requests received no reply.
events.caption: The controller requested an arrival estimate for TASIL. Repeated later requests received no reply.

events.title: Last recorded radar point
events.detail: Radar data show passage of SALPU at the limit of coverage. A numeric coordinate for the radar point is not transcribed in the report passage used here.
events.caption: The aircraft passed SALPU at the edge of radar coverage, marking its last recorded radar position.

events.title: Relief pilot called
events.detail: A call sounded in the flight crew rest facility before the change of crew positions.
events.caption: A call sounded in the crew rest area before the pilots changed positions.

events.title: Relief pilot enters cockpit
events.detail: The relief copilot entered the cockpit. The captain remained for the briefing before leaving.
events.caption: The relief copilot entered the cockpit. The captain stayed for a briefing before leaving.

events.title: Captain leaves for rest
events.detail: The captain left the cockpit and the door closed. Two copilots were then seated at the controls.
events.caption: The captain left to rest, leaving two copilots at the controls.

events.title: Cabin crew warned of turbulence
events.detail: The flying copilot warned the cabin crew that more movement was expected shortly. This was a precautionary interphone call.
events.caption: The flying copilot warned the cabin crew that more turbulence was expected shortly.

events.title: Heading change begins
events.detail: Lateral mode changed to HDG and the selected magnetic heading decreased toward 34°. BEA interpreted the left deviation as probably avoiding weather-radar returns.
events.caption: The aircraft began turning left, probably to avoid weather shown on radar.

events.title: Selected Mach reduced
events.detail: Speed management changed from managed to selected Mach 0.80.
events.caption: The crew switched from automatic speed selection to a chosen speed of Mach 0.80.

events.title: Engine anti-ice selected
events.detail: Engine nacelle anti-ice was selected on. BEA notes four-second sampling: engine 1 was first recorded on at 02:10:05, while selections are normally simultaneous.
events.caption: The crew switched on the system that prevents ice forming on the engine housings.

events.title: Autopilot disconnects
events.detail: Airspeed indications became inconsistent, most likely after ice crystals obstructed the Pitot probes. The aircraft rolled right and the flying copilot made nose-up and lateral inputs.
events.caption: The autopilot disconnected as speed readings disagreed, likely from ice-blocked sensors. The flying copilot made nose-up control inputs.

events.title: Alternate flight-control law
events.detail: Flight control changed from normal to alternate law. This removed normal high-angle-of-attack protection.
events.caption: The flight-control mode changed, removing automatic protection against the wings losing lift at too steep an angle.

events.title: Autothrust disconnects
events.detail: Autothrust disengaged and thrust lock activated. Autopilot and autothrust remained disengaged for the rest of the flight.
events.caption: Automatic engine power control disconnected. It and the autopilot remained off for the rest of the flight.

events.title: First brief stall warning
events.detail: The CVR captured a short stall-warning activation lasting until 02:10:11.3. A second brief activation occurred from 02:10:13 to 02:10:13.4; this was before the sustained stall.
events.caption: Two brief warnings sounded that the wings could lose lift, before the sustained stall began.

events.title: Crew identifies missing speeds
events.detail: The monitoring copilot called out the loss of airspeed indications and alternate law. The crew did not call for the unreliable-airspeed procedure.
events.caption: The monitoring copilot identified missing speed readings. The crew did not call for the procedure for unreliable airspeed.

events.title: Wing anti-ice selected
events.detail: The wing anti-ice selector was moved on while the aircraft was climbing.
events.caption: The crew switched on the wing ice-prevention system while the aircraft was climbing.

events.title: Climb rate reaches maximum
events.detail: Recorded vertical speed reached 6,900 ft/min. Pitch-up inputs had displaced the aircraft from its cruise flight level.
events.caption: Nose-up control inputs took the aircraft above its cruising level. Its climb reached 6,900 feet per minute.

events.title: Left-side speed recovers
events.detail: The left-side airspeed returned to a valid value of about 223 kt after 29 seconds of incorrect indication. The standby speed remained erroneous longer.
events.caption: The left speed display became reliable after 29 seconds. The backup display remained wrong longer.

events.title: Continuous stall warning starts
events.detail: The warning began to sound continuously as angle of attack increased. The flying copilot continued mainly nose-up inputs.
events.caption: The warning of lost wing lift became continuous. The flying copilot continued mainly nose-up control inputs.

events.title: Call toward crew rest
events.detail: The CVR recorded a cabin or flight-rest call chime. Further call signals were sent to the rest facility between 02:11:09.8 and 02:11:27.
events.caption: A call chime sounded for the cabin or crew rest area. Further calls went to the rest area.

events.title: Vibration audible in cockpit
events.detail: Vibration sounds were audible until 02:12:57. BEA associated the approach to stall with warning and buffet.
events.caption: Vibration became audible in the cockpit as the aircraft approached a loss of wing lift.

events.title: Takeoff thrust selected
events.detail: Thrust levers were moved into TOGA. High thrust did not prevent the rising angle of attack and subsequent descent.
events.caption: The crew selected takeoff engine power, but the wing's angle to the airflow kept rising before the descent.

events.title: Standby speed becomes consistent
events.detail: Recorded PFD CAS was 184 kt and ISIS CAS 183 kt. The aircraft was already approaching the top of its climb with a high angle of attack.
events.caption: The main and backup speed readings agreed again as the aircraft neared the top of its climb.

events.title: Highest recorded pressure altitude
events.detail: Standard-pressure altitude reached 37,924 ft. It must not be treated as an exact height above mean sea level.
events.caption: The highest altitude reading reached about 38,000 feet. Its exact height above sea level is unknown.

events.title: Brief sidestick priority change
events.detail: The left-seat copilot took priority. The right-seat copilot took it back shortly afterwards; these changes were not accompanied by clear spoken transfers.
events.locator: Appendix 2 p.5; section 1.1 p.23; prose rounds first action to 02:11:37
events.caption: The copilots briefly switched control priority between them without clear spoken handovers.

events.title: Captain returns
events.detail: The captain returned while the aircraft was descending in a sustained stall. The crew did not establish a shared diagnosis of the stall.
events.caption: The captain returned during the stalled descent. The crew did not agree that the wings had lost lift.

events.title: Stall warning becomes silent
events.detail: All three recorded angles of attack became invalid and the warning stopped after 54 continuous seconds. This silence did not mean that the aircraft had recovered.
events.locator: Appendix 2 p.5; sections 1.16.3.2 p.89 and 3.1 p.198
events.caption: The stall warning stopped when sensor readings became invalid. The aircraft had not recovered.

events.title: Thrust reduced to idle
events.detail: Thrust levers were moved to IDLE. Engine N1 then decreased toward about 58% over twenty seconds.
events.caption: The crew moved the engine power levers to idle. Engine power then decreased.

events.title: Speedbrakes briefly deployed
events.detail: The speedbrakes were commanded and deployed during 02:12:04–02:12:07.
events.caption: The crew briefly deployed the aircraft's air brakes for about three seconds.

events.title: Thrust advanced again
events.detail: Thrust levers were moved to CLB. The engines responded, increasing N1 toward 105%.
events.caption: The crew selected climb power. The engines responded by increasing power.

events.title: Brief full nose-down input
events.detail: The right sidestick was held fully nose-down for two seconds and TOGA thrust was selected. Later temporary valid angle-of-attack readings still exceeded the stall region.
events.caption: The right-seat copilot briefly pushed fully forward and selected takeoff power. Later readings still showed stalled wings.

events.title: Passing near ten thousand feet
events.detail: Recorded pressure altitude was 10,092 ft. The flying copilot referred to approaching flight level 100.
events.caption: The altitude display read about 10,000 feet. The flying copilot mentioned approaching that level.

events.title: Overlapping control inputs
events.detail: During the interval to 02:14:07 the left stick gave mainly nose-down commands, while the right stick alternated full nose-up and neutral. The DUAL INPUT parameter activated five times in that interval.
events.caption: Both copilots made overlapping inputs, with the left mostly commanding nose-down and the right alternating nose-up and neutral.

events.title: Final thrust reduction
events.detail: Thrust levers were selected IDLE for two seconds and then moved forward. They were advanced toward TOGA again during 02:14:18–02:14:21.
events.caption: The crew briefly reduced engine power to idle, then increased it and later moved toward takeoff power again.

events.title: Ground-proximity warnings begin
events.detail: The GPWS sounded sink-rate and then pull-up warnings. The chronology gives radio altitude 2,140 ft at this time.
events.caption: Warnings sounded about rapid descent and the need to pull up, about 2,140 feet above the sea.

events.title: High angle of attack persists
events.detail: One valid channel-2 reading was 41.1°. The right-seat pilot took sidestick priority through the end of the flight.
events.caption: The wing's angle to the airflow remained steep. The right-seat copilot took control priority until the flight ended.

events.title: Recording ends near ocean impact
events.detail: BEA times impact to 02:14:28 and recording end to 02:14:28.4; exact subsecond contact time is not established here. The last sampled pitch was 16.2° nose-up, bank 5.3° left and vertical speed -10,912 ft/min. The aircraft was intact until impact.
events.locator: Appendix 2 p.9; synopsis p.17; sections 1.1 p.24 and 1.12.4 p.81
events.caption: The recording ended near ocean impact. The aircraft remained intact until impact, descending rapidly with its nose raised.

events.title: Search process initiated
events.detail: Atlantico–Recife ARCC registered the disappearance and began gathering flight information. Formal alerting and search deployment were delayed by failures in flight monitoring and coordination.
events.caption: Rescue coordination began gathering flight information. Failures in monitoring and coordination delayed alerts and search deployment.

events.title: First confirmed surface recovery
events.detail: French and Brazilian forces began recovering confirmed wreckage and victims on 6 June. Time of day is not established here.
events.caption: French and Brazilian forces began recovering wreckage and victims from the sea on June 6.

events.title: Search strategy reassessed
events.detail: Metron’s report combined flight-dynamics priors, uncertain reverse-drift estimates and earlier unsuccessful searches. This was a probability map for locating wreckage, not a reconstructed flight path.
events.caption: A new search map combined likely aircraft movements, uncertain drift estimates, and earlier unsuccessful searches to locate wreckage.

events.title: Main wreckage located
events.detail: BEA’s investigation chronology dates the discovery to 3 April 2011 at about 3,900 m depth. The final-report prose instead says 2 April; both dates are retained in conflicts. Time of day is unknown here.
events.locator: BEA chronology; final report sections 1.1 p.24 and 1.12.1 p.65
events.caption: The main wreckage was found about 3,900 meters below the sea. The exact discovery date is uncertain.

events.title: Flight data recorder recovered
events.detail: The FDR protected memory unit was recovered from the seabed. The BEA chronology distinguishes discovery on 1 May from recovery on 2 May.
events.caption: The flight recorder's protected memory unit was recovered from the seabed, a day after it was found.

events.title: Cockpit recorder recovered
events.detail: The CVR was discovered and recovered. Both recorders were later read in France.
events.caption: The cockpit voice recorder was recovered. Both recorders were later read in France.

events.title: BEA final report published
events.detail: BEA explained the air-data failure, inappropriate control inputs and failure to recognize and recover from the stall. It also identified training, feedback, interface and crew-coordination weaknesses.
events.caption: The investigation linked faulty speed readings, control inputs, and an unrecognized stall, identifying training and crew-coordination weaknesses.

events.title: Companies acquitted at first trial
events.detail: The Paris criminal court acquitted Airbus and Air France. Prosecutors appealed on 27 April 2023; this acquittal was later reversed on appeal.
events.locator: Points clés, dates clés de la procédure
events.caption: Airbus and Air France were acquitted at the first criminal trial. The acquittals were later reversed on appeal.

events.title: Appeal trial opens
events.detail: The official court chronology gives the appeal hearings as 29 September to 27 November 2025. No time of day is supplied.
events.locator: Points clés, dates clés de la procédure
events.caption: The appeal hearings began on September 29, 2025, and continued through November 27.

events.title: Appeal court convicts both companies
events.detail: The Paris Court of Appeal convicted Airbus and Air France of involuntary homicide and fined each €225,000. This legal ruling does not change the recorded flight path.
events.locator: Points clés: infractions retenues and tableau des condamnations
events.caption: The appeal court convicted Airbus and Air France of involuntary homicide, fining each company €225,000.

events.title: Airbus announces cassation appeal
events.detail: Airbus announced that it would seek review by the Court of Cassation. No subsequent AF447 cassation outcome was located in searches through 7 November 2026.
events.caption: Airbus announced plans to seek a further court review. The outcome is unknown.

perspectives.label: Loss of control and stall
perspectives.claim: Temporary airspeed disagreement most likely followed ice-crystal obstruction of the Pitot probes. Control inputs caused a climb and exit from the flight envelope, followed by a stall that the crew did not diagnose or recover from; training, feedback and cockpit-interface weaknesses contributed.

evidence_for.text: FDR shows nose-up inputs, a climb to pressure altitude 37,924 ft, then high angle of attack and rapid descent; Appendix 2.
Flight controls followed crew commands and engines responded normally; warning, buffet and crew communications support the failure to identify the stall; final report sections 1.12.4 and 3.

evidence_against.text: The ice crystals themselves were not sampled. The precise reason for each pilot’s actions cannot be recovered from the recorder alone; the report describes the Pitot obstruction as likely.

ending.description: Recorded sustained-stall descent to the Atlantic. No competing recorded endpoint exists.

perspectives.label: Airbus disputes criminal liability
perspectives.claim: Airbus contests the conviction and announced a cassation appeal. It cites the 2019 dismissal and 2023 acquittal as earlier decisions in its favour; this is a legal defence, not an alternative physical flight path.

evidence_for.text: Earlier dismissal and acquittal are documented in the official court chronology, although subsequently overturned in the relevant stages of proceedings.
The BEA found the flight controls followed pilot commands and the engines functioned normally; these facts establish mechanical responses but do not decide corporate criminal liability.

evidence_against.text: The 2026 appeal court convicted both companies of involuntary homicide.
The BEA identified failures in risk feedback, high-altitude handling training and warning ergonomics in addition to crew inputs; section 3.2.

ending.description: Same recorded ending. Responsibility, rather than location or aircraft motion, is contested.

perspectives.label: Early lightning explanation
perspectives.held_by: Air France’s communications director, as reported on 1 June 2009
perspectives.claim: Early public statements suggested a lightning strike could have caused the loss. This preceded recovery of the recorders and is not supported as the accident’s causal explanation by the completed investigation.

evidence_for.text: There were powerful convective clouds along the route, so electrical activity was physically possible; final report section 1.7.
The early lightning suggestion is documented in the contemporaneous Scientific American article; it is not an established observation of a strike.

evidence_against.text: Recorders establish airspeed disagreement, control inputs and a prolonged stall; the systems and engines continued responding.
BEA found no evidence of fire or explosion and concluded that the aircraft was intact at impact; sections 1.12.4 and 1.14. Those findings do not prove no harmless strike occurred.

ending.description: No defensible alternative lightning-caused path or impact time was published in the source used; no track override is invented.

evidence_points.label: Last transmitted ACARS position
evidence_points.detail: FM position tagged 02:10, received at 02:10:34. Coordinates were sent to two decimal places. This is a flight-position anchor, not the impact site; s4 section 1.16.2.

evidence_points.label: BEA accident and wreckage reference
evidence_points.detail: Synopsis reference converted from 3°03′57″ N, 30°33′42″ W. Approximate wreckage-area anchor at about 3,900 m depth, not an exact surveyed surface impact coordinate. Decimal conversion only; s1 synopsis and section 1.12.1.

evidence_points.label: Centre of initial search circle
evidence_points.detail: BEA considered a 40 NM radius around the last known position. Metron used this as part of its prior probability distribution, with historical loss-of-control distances and uncertain reverse-drift information; s12 sections 3.1–3.3. The centre is not a second observation.
evidence_points.method: Metron, Stone et al., section 3.1: a uniform 40 NM radius prior centred on the last ACARS position, mixed with a historical loss-of-control distance prior. This point marks the circle centre, not an observed crash location.

witnesses.who: Flight crew of preceding Lufthansa LH507
witnesses.said: Paraphrase: About twenty minutes ahead at FL350, they flew near the cloud tops and then in cloud near ORARO. They avoided radar returns about ten nautical miles west, felt moderate turbulence, saw no lightning and heard no AF447 call on 121.5 MHz. This describes a different flight path and time, not conditions proven aboard AF447 (s1 section 1.18.5.1 p.158).

Paraphrase: He observed passage of SALPU at 01:49 on his radar display. He expected further position reports and did not call by SELCAL; controllers described poor HF communications that night (s1 section 1.18.5.2 pp.158–159).

numbers.label: Continuous warning of lost wing lift

why_it_matters: The accident led to Pitot-probe restrictions and changes to high-altitude manual-flight and unreliable-airspeed training (s1, sections 5.1–5.3, pp.215–217). It exposed weaknesses in stall recognition, cockpit warnings, crew coordination and oceanic tracking (s1, sections 3–4). EASA’s 2025 guidance explicitly links relief-commander CRM training and experience guidance to AF447 recommendations (s11, pp.4–5).

conflicts.about: ORARO estimate in the last position report
conflicts.a: First interim report section 1.1 gives ORARO estimated at 02:00 in the 01:35:15 position report.
conflicts.b: Final report section 1.9.1 p.49 gives ORARO estimated at 02:04. Neither estimate is used as a measured aircraft position.

conflicts.a: Final report sections 1.1 p.24 and 1.12.1 p.65 say 2 April 2011.
conflicts.b: BEA investigation chronology says 3 April 2011. The exact sonar-detection versus confirmation or announcement basis was not reconciled here; no time of day is invented.

conflicts.a: Appendix 1 p.2 and Appendix 2 p.1 give 00:09:14.
conflicts.b: Final report section 1.11.2 p.58 says 00:09:15. The track uses the timestamp printed beside the Appendix 2 initial values.

conflicts.a: Appendix 2 p.6 explicitly dates the later CAS peak of 127 kt to 02:12:53.
conflicts.b: Appendix 2 p.7 describes the interval 02:12:52–02:12:57 as beginning at 127 kt. The track uses the explicit peak timestamp and does not assume sub-second precision.

conflicts.a: Final report section 1.1 p.23 places the left-seat copilot’s takeover at 02:11:37.
conflicts.b: Appendix 2 p.5 lists recorded priority at 02:11:38. The event uses the discrete FDR chronology time and preserves the prose discrepancy.

conflicts.a: The 2023 criminal trial ended in acquittal; Airbus continues to contest responsibility and announced a cassation appeal in May 2026.
conflicts.b: The Paris Court of Appeal convicted both companies on 21 May 2026. This is a legal disagreement and change of judgment, not conflicting recorder data.

conflicts.about: Early lightning explanation versus recovered evidence
conflicts.a: An Air France spokesperson initially suggested lightning, as contemporaneously reported.
conflicts.b: The final BEA causal sequence is Pitot-related speed disagreement, control inputs and an unrecognized sustained stall. A lightning strike was not established as its cause.

unknowns: A raw numerical FDR export with continuous latitude/longitude, attitude, speed and altitude was not obtained. BEA publishes selected values and parameter graphs. The opened public materials do not provide a transcribed dense coordinate table; the last minutes therefore have null airborne positions.

True geometric altitude above mean sea level is not established at the recorder timestamps. Standard-pressure altitude and radio height are preserved in added fields; local pressure/temperature structure needed for a true-altitude conversion was not found. Some early pressure-altitude changes are air-data artifacts.
Exact second at which the last ACARS position was sampled is unknown. Its payload is tagged 02:10 and receipt was 02:10:34; receipt time is not silently used as measurement time.

Exact sea-surface impact coordinates, seabed descent or drift of each heavy component, and component-level surveyed coordinates were not numerically recovered here. The site uses BEA’s synopsis reference with approximate precision.
Historical coordinates for the filed route fixes and TASIL were not verified from the 2009 navigation database or AIP. They remain null. Modern fix positions were not substituted.
Some instantaneous pitch, roll, angle of attack, speed and engine values are absent from the selected chronology. Interval ranges were not converted into invented samples or sinusoidal motion.

During much of the stall, airspeed and angle-of-attack parameters were NCD or FW. Exact true airspeed and a continuous valid angle-of-attack history cannot be recovered by treating invalid values as zero.

The exact continuous right-seat PFD airspeed is not separately recorded. The FDR CAS source could switch when a PFD value was invalid; this switch is not explicit in the parameter (s1 section 1.11.2 p.59).
The reason angle-of-attack channel 1 behaved more slowly than the other channels was not established by BEA; the report says it did not affect system functioning (s1 p.90).

No direct sample established the ice-crystal size distribution, ice water content, liquid-water fraction or exact Pitot obstruction history along this aircraft’s path. Ice-crystal obstruction is the BEA’s likely explanation, not a recovered physical ice sample.

Cloud bases, exact true-MSL cloud tops, coverage in oktas, in-cloud visibility and a measured full wind vector at the accident aircraft were not numerically established. Forecast flight levels and satellite-derived top estimates are retained in notes rather than passed off as direct local observations.

Impact-time surface wind, sea state, wave height, precipitation at sea level and moon visibility were not established by the weather/search documents reviewed. Later search conditions and regional wind bounds are not substituted.
A harmless lightning strike cannot be ruled in or out from the material used; the later absence of satellite-detected lightning does not prove there was none at the time of the accident.

The pilots’ exact mental models and reasons for individual inputs cannot be known from recorded speech and controls alone. No cabin witness survived; nearby-flight testimony is not direct observation of AF447’s impact.

The one-day disagreement in the BEA wreckage-discovery dates was not reconciled from an opened operation log. The search-operations PDF was linked but exceeded the web fetch size limit and direct BEA downloads timed out; final-report site data, the BEA chronology and the opened Metron report were used instead.

A directly verified wing-sweep value with its reference convention was not found in the primary aircraft documents inspected, so wing_sweep_deg is null. Exact serial-specific dimensions and accident-day repaint status were not established; type dimensions and a dated May 2009 photograph are explicitly identified.

The full reasoned May 2026 court judgment and any later AF447 cassation disposition were not obtained. The opened court key-points notice and Airbus statement support the recorded legal developments; searches covered 2024–2026 through 7 November 2026.
Times of day for the post-accident discovery, recovery, publication and court events are unknown here. Day-only date_utc fields preserve the known dates without invented midnight timestamps.
memorial_note: We remember the 216 passengers and 12 crew members who died, and the families and communities who carry their loss.

sources.title: Final report: accident on 1 June 2009 to Airbus A330-203 F-GZCP, AF447
sources.publisher: BEA; official copy hosted by US Federal Aviation Administration
sources.notes: Downloaded with curl and all 224 PDF pages extracted with PyMuPDF. Printed page numbers are two less than PDF page numbers. English translation; French is the reference text. Main locations: synopsis p.17; history pp.21–24; aircraft pp.30–31; weather pp.46–47; recorder interpretation pp.57–60; wreckage pp.64–81; aircraft simulations pp.88–92; testimony pp.156–159; conclusions pp.197–201; safety actions pp.215–217. All report times are UTC; synopsis footnote gives Rio time as UTC minus three hours and metropolitan France as UTC plus two hours on the accident date.

sources.title: Final report Appendix 2: Chronologie FDR
sources.notes: Opened as a nine-page official PDF through the web reader, including the initial-state table, second-specific chronology and last-value table. French original. These are selected recorded values and interval descriptions, not a downloadable raw time-series table. Later direct curl/reopen attempts timed out; the document was nevertheless successfully opened and read. Printed appendix page numbers are used as locators.

sources.title: Final report Appendix 1: CVR Transcript, English translation
sources.notes: Opened official 32-page PDF. Foreword cautions that a CVR is only a partial reflection of cockpit events. UTC comes from FDR synchronization. No private conversations or verbatim crew quotations are reproduced here. Detailed final-flight CVR event times below are taken from the final report section 1.11.2 where indicated. Appendix p.2 starts at 00:09:14, differing by one second from final-report prose.

sources.title: First interim report, English translation
sources.notes: Downloaded with curl and text extracted from 72 PDF pages. This mirror contains the main English report without the separate French appendices; its pagination differs from the longer BEA edition. Section 1.16.2.2 at printed p.45 gives the last ACARS coordinates and receipt time; section 1.16.2.4 reproduces the message payload. Only primary BEA content is used, not commentary by the mirror host.

sources.title: Premier rapport d’étape, including Appendix 1 Météo-France meteorological study
sources.publisher: BEA / Météo-France; document mirrored by AirSafe.com
sources.notes: Downloaded with curl; all 129 PDF pages extracted with PyMuPDF. Appendix 1 pp.75–93 is the primary Météo-France study; sections 1.1–1.4 cover wind and tropopause, 2.3 satellite analysis and 3 limitations. Appendix 6 p.113 gives the filed ATC flight plan. Original physical document, despite the mirror web-reader title. The original BEA first-interim PDF was also opened at https://bea.aero/fileadmin/documents/docspa/2009/f-cp090601e1.en/pdf/f-cp090601e1.en.pdf .

sources.title: AF447 investigation page and investigation chronology
sources.notes: Opened the official investigation page, report/appendix links and dated search chronology. Live page checked in November 2026. Lists discovery on 3 April 2011, FDR recovery on 2 May and CVR recovery on 3 May. Page publication/revision year is not established; the year field is null.

sources.title: A330-200: dimensions
sources.notes: Opened manufacturer type page. Dimensions section gives length 58.82 m, span 60.3 m, height 17.39 m and external fuselage width 5.64 m. These are published type dimensions, not an as-built measurement of F-GZCP. The same main dimensions were cross-checked in the opened Airbus April 2026 facts-and-figures PDF. Publication year is unknown. Accessed November 2026. Do not transfer modern weights or range to the accident aircraft.

sources.title: OurAirports airport data: airports.csv
sources.notes: Downloaded successfully with curl and parsed the LFPG and SBGL rows locally; the web reader cannot display text/csv. Airport reference coordinates and elevations are current database values, not historical runway thresholds or recorded aircraft positions. Accessed 7 November 2026.

sources.title: Arrêt du 21 mai 2026, Rio-Paris: points clés
sources.notes: Opened official court PDF. One-page key-points notice records convictions, fines and procedural dates. It is a court summary, not the complete reasoned judgment. The separate press-release URL returned a maintenance page, so its unseen contents are not used.

sources.title: AF447 Flight: Airbus to lodge appeal with the Court of Cassation following Paris Court of Appeal decision
sources.notes: Opened company statement dated 21 May 2026. Primary evidence of Airbus’s position and announced appeal, not an independent determination of responsibility. Searches through 7 November 2026 did not locate a subsequent AF447 cassation disposition; absence of a search result is not proof that no later filing exists.

sources.title: Annex VII to ED Decision 2025/002/R: AMC and GM to Part-ORO, Issue 2 Amendment 26
sources.notes: Opened six-page EASA PDF. Pages 3–4 explicitly trace relief-commander CRM training and minimum-experience guidance to AF447 recommendations. This is AMC/GM guidance; the recommended 3,000 hours is not described here as an absolute regulatory minimum.

sources.title: Search Analysis for the Location of the AF447 Underwater Wreckage
sources.publisher: Metron: Lawrence D. Stone, Colleen Keller, Thomas L. Kratzke and Johan Strumpfer; report to BEA
sources.notes: Opened 43-page primary technical report dated 20 January 2011. Sections 2–4 explain the Bayesian search, historical loss-of-control distance prior and reverse-drift uncertainties. These search probability distributions are not aircraft flight paths. No invented representative path has been extracted from them.

sources.title: Could lightning have brought down Air France Flight 447?
sources.notes: Opened article dated 1 June 2009. Used only to document the early lightning suggestion attributed to Air France’s communications director. Its preliminary times and technical speculation are not used for the reconstruction.

sources.title: F-GZCP Aircraft.jpg, photograph taken 2 May 2009
sources.notes: Opened description page, downloaded original JPEG and inspected it visually. Photograph is dated 2 May 2009, not the accident day. White fuselage, dark blue AIR FRANCE titles and blue/white/red diagonal tail stripes are visible. Livery continuity to 31 May is not independently documented.

data_notes.time_basis: UTC throughout. Minute-resolution times are written without invented seconds. Day-only post-accident events have t_utc null and an added date_utc; their time of day is unknown. Event ordering uses t_utc or date_utc.
data_notes.altitude_basis: alt_ft is reserved for actual MSL altitude and remains null where unavailable. Added pressure_alt_ft preserves BEA standard-pressure altitude (1013.25 hPa), including erroneous transients during Pitot icing. Added radio_alt_ft preserves height above the reflecting surface. Neither is silently relabelled MSL. There is insufficient atmospheric data for a defensible true-altitude conversion.
data_notes.airspeed_basis: ias_kt preserves the BEA CAS parameter displayed as airspeed on the PFD, rather than a mechanically uncorrected IAS or true airspeed. Added isis_cas_kt is the standby-display parameter. Recorded numbers are retained even when erroneous; airspeed_status and method identify them. Invalid NCD/FW values are null, never zero-filled. See s1 section 1.11.2 p.59.
data_notes.angle_basis: Positive pitch is nose-up; positive roll is right bank. hdg_deg is magnetic heading where populated, not true course or a selected heading. aoa_deg uses channel 2 unless stated otherwise; added aoa_channels_deg retains the separate channels when explicit.
data_notes.sampling: Only explicit numerical values and named interval endpoints in the published FDR chronology are included. No time-series curve has been invented or interpolated. The underlying raw recorder file was not obtained. Samples in one row may have different recording phases; final values do not prove exact simultaneity at contact with the sea.
data_notes.positions: The only airborne coordinate pair transcribed numerically is the last minute-tagged ACARS position. Airport reference points and wreckage coordinates are not substituted into the airborne track. A complete spatial trajectory cannot be reconstructed from these sparse numeric anchors alone.
data_notes.route_scope: The planned_waypoints array transcribes named fixes in the filed ATC plan in s5 appendix 6 p.113, excluding airways and alternate route instructions. TASIL is an additional oceanic reporting/FIR-boundary point discussed in s1; its historical coordinates are unknown here. The filed step-climb plan was not the same as the actual FL350 flight.
data_notes.geometry: Airframe dimensions are Airbus type-level published dimensions. No serial-specific dimensional survey was obtained. External fuselage width is used for the requested diameter field.
